parts.problem_md:
This question is about the elements in Group 7.

Use your knowledge of the trends in the properties of Group 7 elements to predict the colour and physical state of astatine at room temperature.
parts.solution_md:
Predicting the colour and physical state of astatine at room temperature:

- (Dark) grey / black 
**AND** 
Solid; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The halogens become darker as you go down the group*
- *Astatine is at the bottom of the group, so will be darker than iodine, which is grey*
- *Their melting points and boiling points also increase so the elements toward the bottom of the group, i.e. iodine and astatine, will be solid at room temperature*

parts.problem_md:
i) State the meaning of the term electronegativity.

**(1)**

ii) Explain the trend in electronegativity down Group 7.

**(2)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The meaning of the term electronegativity is:

- The ability of an atom to attract a bonding / shared pair of electrons (in a covalent bond) 
**OR** 
The ability of an atom to attract electrons in a covalent bond; **[1 mark]**

ii) The trend in electronegativity down Group 7 is:

- Elements become less electronegative (down the group); **[1 mark]**
- The outer electron(s) / shell is further away from the (positive) nucleus (so the bonding electrons are less strongly attracted); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *There are a few alternative ways to explain why the electronegativity of Group 7 elements decreases down the group that you would be awarded a mark for, these are:*

  - *There is an increased repulsion (from inner electrons)*
  - *There is more shielding (by inner electrons)*
  - *There are more (inner) shells of electrons*
  - *The effective nuclear charge is lower*

parts.problem_md:
Compare and contrast the reactions of chlorine with

- water
- cold, dilute aqueous alkali
- hot, concentrated aqueous alkali

Include an equation for each reaction, stating the type of reaction and the oxidation numbers of the chlorine involved. State symbols are not required.
parts.solution_md:
To compare and contrast the reactions of chlorine:

**Chemical ideas expressed **

- All are disproportionation reactions (because chlorine is both oxidised and reduced)
- Chlorine changes / is reduced from 0 to ‒1 (in Cl– in all reactions)
- Cl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ HCl + HOCl
**OR**
Cl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>‒</sup> + HOCl
- Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → NaClO + NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O
**OR**
Cl<sub>2 </sub>+ 2OH<sup>‒</sup> → ClO<sup>‒</sup> + Cl<sup>‒</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O
- 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6NaOH → NaClO<sub>3</sub> + 5NaCl + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
**OR**
3Cl<sub>2 </sub>+ 6OH<sup>‒</sup> → ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>‒</sup> + 5Cl<sup>‒</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
- Chlorine oxidised to +1 (in HOCl), +1 (in NaClO  and +5 (in NaClO<sub>3</sub>) shown in the appropriate reaction

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *An answer scoring** 6** marks would include*

  - *6 correct marking points AND answer is written in a clear and logical order and points fully explained *
- *An answer scoring** 5** marks would include*

  - *5-4 correct marking points AND answer is written in a clear and logical order and points fully explained *
- *An answer scoring** 4** marks would include*

  - *4-3 correct marking points AND answer has some structure and gives some explained points*
- *An answer scoring **3** marks would include*

  - *3-2 correct marking points AND answer has some structure and gives some explained points*

parts.problem_md:
This question is about redox chemistry, Group 2 and Group 7.

When chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium bromide, the solution turns orange.

State the changes in oxidation number of bromine and chlorine, and identify which species is the oxidising agent.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The changes in oxidation number are:
> 
> - Chlorine: 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) → −1 (in Cl<sup>-</sup>)
> **AND**
> Bromine: −1 (in Br<sup>-</sup>) → 0 (in Br<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The oxidising agent is:
> 
> - Chlorine / Cl<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Chloride ions / Cl<sup>-</sup> is not accepted for the oxidising agent

> **[exam-tip]**
> The orange colour in solution confirms Br<sub>2</sub> has formed. Purple colouration would indicate I<sub>2</sub> in cyclohexane, which belongs to a different halide displacement reaction.
> 
> Three errors to watch for in this question:
> 
> 1. Reverse-direction equations:
> 
>   - Br<sub>2</sub> + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> → 2Br<sup>-</sup> + Cl<sub>2</sub> is chemically impossible
> 2. Unsigned oxidation numbers:
> 
>   - Writing "1" instead of "−1" will not score
> 3. Confusing oxidising and reducing agents:
> 
>   - The **oxidising agent** is itself **reduced** (gains electrons).
>   - Memory aid: **OIL RIG** (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).

parts.problem_md: Describe and explain the trend in thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates (MgCO<sub>3</sub> to BaCO<sub>3</sub>).
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend for Group 2 carbonate thermal stability is:
> 
> - Thermal stability increases down the group
> **OR**
> Decomposition temperature increases down the group **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The size/radius of the cation increases but has the same charge (so charge density decreases)
> **OR**
> The calcium ion is larger than magnesium ion **[1 mark]**
> - So the cation is less polarising / distorts the electron cloud of the carbonate ion less (weakening the C–O bond less)
> **OR**
> The covalent character of M–O bond decreases, which distorts the electron cloud of the carbonate ion less (weakening the C–O bond less) **[1 mark]**.
> 
> Vague references to "the ion" without specifying which ion polarises which are not accepted for the second mark.
> 
> Answers that talk about polarising the molecule or atom are not accepted for the third mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Group 2 carbonate thermal stability is a common paper discriminator. The January 2022 examiner report noted: "We regularly saw 'thermal decomposition decreases down the group'. This response fails to score as it does not refer to either the temperature of decomposition or the thermal stability. Many candidates referred to polarisation of the ion, without specifying which ion was polarising which."
> 
> To score all three marks, state explicitly:
> 
> 1. Cation size increases down the group
> 2. Cation polarising power decreases
> 3. The carbonate anion is distorted less
> 4. A higher temperature is therefore required to decompose the carbonate

parts.problem_md:
A 1.25 g sample of impure limestone is analysed to find its percentage of calcium carbonate by a back-titration method.

![Laboratory setup showing a burette clamped to a stand above a conical flask, both partly filled with liquid, used for titration experiments](assets/001-laboratory-setup-showing-a-burette-clamped-to-a-.png)

The sample is dissolved in 50.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.500 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> hydrochloric acid (an excess).

The excess hydrochloric acid is then titrated against 0.200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> sodium hydroxide solution. The volume required to neutralise the excess acid is 25.00 cm<sup>3</sup>.

[Assume the impurities in the limestone do not react with the hydrochloric acid. *M*<sub>r</sub>(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 100.0]

Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the limestone sample.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the limestone sample:

- Calculate the initial moles of HCl added and the moles of NaOH used (equal to the moles of excess HCl)

moles = concentration x volume (dm<sup>3</sup>)

*n*(HCl<sub>start</sub>) = 0.500 x $\frac{50.0}{1000}$
*n*(HCl<sub>start</sub>) = 0.0250 mol

*n*(NaOH) = 0.200 x $\frac{25.0}{1000}$

*n*(NaOH) = 0.00500 mol = *n*(HCl<sub>excess</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of HCl that reacted with CaCO<sub>3</sub> by subtraction:

*n*(HCl<sub>reacted</sub>) = 0.0250 − 0.00500

*n*(HCl<sub>reacted</sub>) = 0.0200 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of CaCO<sub>3:</sub>

  - Apply the 1:2 stoichiometric ratio from CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>:

*n*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = $\frac{0.0200}{2}$ 
*n*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = = 0.0100 mol

- Calculate the mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub>:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

*m*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 0.0100 x 100.0

*m*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 1.00 g **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage by mass:

percentage by mass = `fraction numerator m open parentheses CaCO subscript 3 close parentheses over denominator total space sample space mass end fraction` x 100

% CaCO<sub>3</sub> = $\frac{1.00}{1.25}$ x 100

% CaCO<sub>3</sub> = **80.0%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for initial moles of HCl = 0.0250 mol, showing *c* x *V* with volume converted to dm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> 1 mark for moles of NaOH = 0.00500 mol, correctly identified as the moles of excess HCl.
> 
> 1 mark for moles of HCl that reacted with CaCO<sub>3</sub> by subtraction: 0.0250 − 0.00500 = 0.0200 mol.
> 
> 1 mark for moles and mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> using the 1:2 stoichiometric ratio: *n*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 0.0100 mol, *m*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 1.00 g.
> 
> 1 mark for final answer 80.0% or 80%, including the % symbol.
> 
> Allow error carried forward across steps: if a step is wrong but the subsequent method is correct, later marks can still be awarded.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The core principle of back-titration is:
> 
> **n(reacted) = n(added) − n(remaining)**
> 
> The most common error is using the titre (moles of NaOH used) as the moles that reacted with CaCO<sub>3</sub>, skipping the subtraction step entirely.
> 
> The CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl reaction has a 1:2 ratio. Always write out the balanced equation and check the stoichiometry before dividing. A 1:1 ratio is the second most common error in this question type.
> 
> In percentage-by-mass questions, remember to divide by the **sample mass** (1.25 g), not by the mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> alone.

parts.problem_md:
When chlorine is bubbled through cold, dilute sodium hydroxide solution, a disproportionation reaction occurs.

Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H<sub>2</sub>O

Explain why it is classified as disproportionation.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is classified as disproportionation because:
> 
> - Chlorine in Cl<sub>2</sub> starts at oxidation number 0 and is simultaneously reduced to −1 (in NaCl) **AND **oxidised to +1 (in NaClO)
> **OR**
> The same element (Cl) in the same starting species (Cl<sub>2</sub>) is both oxidised and reduced in the reaction **[1 mark]**
> 
> "Oxidation and reduction in the same reaction" without specifying the same element is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Your disproportionation explanation needs three components:
> 
> 1. The **same element** (Cl)
> 2. In the **same starting species** (Cl<sub>2</sub>)
> 3. Simultaneously **oxidised AND reduced**
> 
> A common slip is writing "oxidation and reduction in one reaction." That covers every redox reaction, so it will not earn the disproportionation mark.

parts.problem_md: Which statement about the Group 7 elements chlorine, bromine and iodine is **not** correct?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Going down Group 7 reactivity decreases
- This is because the atoms become larger as you move down Group 7

  - This means that there is more shielding by electrons of the positive nucleus
  - This makes making it harder for them to gain an electron and form a 1- ion

**A** is incorrect as  boiling temperature does increase down the group

**C** is incorrect as  first ionisation energy does decrease down the group

**D** is incorrect as  electronegativity does decrease down the group

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: boiling temperature increases down the group

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: first ionisation energy decreases down the group

parts.problem_md: Which silver halides are soluble in **concentrated **aqueous ammonia?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- Silver chloride is soluble in both dilute and concentrated ammonia
- Silver bromide is soluble in concentrated ammonia only
- Silver iodide is insoluble in both dilute and concentrated ammonia

**A** is incorrect as AgBr will be soluble but not AgI

**B** is incorrect as  AgCl will be soluble but not AgI

**D** is incorrect as AgBr will also be soluble

parts.problem_md:
This question is about the reaction of potassium iodide with concentrated sulfuric acid.

Which of these would **not **be seen?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The reaction of sodium iodide and concentrated sulfuric acid is:

  - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) + KI (s) → HI (g) + KHSO<sub>4 </sub>(s)
  - HI is seen as misty fumes
- Sulfuric acid oxidises the hydrogen iodide to several extents:

  - The concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises HI and is itself reduced to sulfur dioxide gas:
  
    - 2HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) → I<sub>2 </sub>(g) + SO<sub>2 </sub>(g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
    - Iodine is seen as a violet/purple vapour
  - The concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises HI and is itself reduced to sulfur:
  
    - 6HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) → 3I<sub>2 </sub>(g) + S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
    - Sulfur is seen as a yellow solid
  - The concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises HI and is itself reduced to hydrogen sulfide:
  
    - 8HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) → 4I<sub>2 </sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
    - Hydrogen sulfide has a strong smell of bad eggs
  - On cooling, I<sub>2</sub> (s) is formed which is a black solid

**A** is incorrect as  the reaction produces misty fumes of HI

**B** is incorrect as the reaction produces the black solid I<sub>2</sub>

**C** is incorrect as the reaction produces the yellow solid S

parts.problem_md: One of the reaction products is the gas H<sub>2</sub>S. What is the **change** in oxidation number of sulfur as H<sub>2</sub>S forms?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The oxidation number of sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is +6
- The oxidation number of sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>S is -2
- The change in oxidation number is (-2) - (+6) = -8

**B** is incorrect as -6 is the change in oxidation number when S (s) forms

**C** is incorrect as  -2 is the oxidation number of S in H<sub>2</sub>S

**D** is incorrect as +6 is the oxidation number of S in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

parts.problem_md: Which of these** increases **as Group 7 is descended?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Halide ions act as reducing agents as they can donate electrons to other species:

  - 2X<sup>-</sup> → X<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>
- As you go down the group, the ionic radius increases and the attraction between the outer electrons and the nucleus decreases
- Therefore the larger the halide ions, the more readily they will lose their outer electron, so their reducing ability increases down the group
- This is demonstrated by the halogen displacement reactions where a more reactive halogen will displace a less reactive halogen from a halide solution of the less reactive halogen

  - Iodide ions lose their electrons more easily than bromide ions
  - Bromide ions lose their electrons more easily than chloride ions

**A** is incorrect as  the oxidising ability of the molecular halogens decreases down the group

**C** is incorrect as  the electrostatic attraction between nucleus and outer shell of electrons decreases down the group

**D** is incorrect as electronegativity decreases down the group

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: oxidising ability of the molecular halogens

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: reducing ability of the halide ions

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and outer shell of electrons

parts.problem_md: When iodine is dissolved in a non-polar organic solvent, the solution formed is
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- An organic solvent, such as cyclohexane can be used to distinguish between bromine and iodine solutions

  - Bromine forms an orange solution
  - Iodine forms a purple solution

**B** is incorrect as  this is the colour of bromine in water

**C** is incorrect as  the solution is not colourless

**D** is incorrect as  the solution is not brown

parts.problem_md:
Four tests used to identify ions are shown:

1   flame test
2   addition of acidified barium nitrate solution
3   addition of acidified silver nitrate solution
4   addition of sodium hydroxide solution, then testing any gas with indicator paper

Which tests could be used to positively identify the ions in ammonium chloride?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Addition of acidified silver nitrate solution to ammonium chloride will form a white precipitate of silver chloride, thus identifying chloride ions
- When sodium hydroxide solution is added to ammonium chloride, ammonia gas is produced which will change the colour of the indicator paper, thus identifying ammonium ions

**A** is incorrect as  a flame test will not positively identify ammonium ions and barium nitrate will not positively identify chloride ions

**B** is incorrect as  a flame test will not positively identify ammonium ions

**C** is incorrect as  barium nitrate will not positively identify chloride ions

parts.problem_md:
Solid potassium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid.

Which of these substances does **not** form?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- When potassium bromide and sulfuric acid react:

  - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) + NaBr (s) → **HBr** (g) + NaHSO<sub>4 </sub>(s)
- The sulfuric acid then oxidises HBr which decomposes to form bromine, hydrogen gas and sulfur dioxide

  - 2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) →** Br**<sub>**2 **</sub>(g) + **SO**<sub>**2**</sub><sub> </sub>(g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
- Hydrogen sulfide is not produced in either reaction
- A reddish brown gas of Br<sub>2</sub> would be observed
- You must also be able to give the observations and equations for the reaction between sulfuric acid, and chloride / iodide ions

**A** is incorrect as  bromine is formed

**B** is incorrect as  hydrogen bromide is formed

**D** is incorrect as  sulfur dioxide is formed

parts.problem_md:
A student adds chlorine water to an aqueous solution of an unknown potassium halide. A small volume of cyclohexane (density = 0.79 g cm<sup>–3</sup>) is then added and the mixture is shaken thoroughly.

The upper layer turns purple/violet.

Which halide was present in the original solution?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Oxidising ability of halogens decreases down Group 7: Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub>
- Cl<sub>2</sub> can therefore oxidise Br<sup>–</sup> and I<sup>–</sup>, but cannot oxidise F<sup>–</sup> (F is above Cl) or Cl<sup>–</sup> (same element, no redox)
- Cyclohexane (density 0.79 g cm<sup>–³</sup>) is less dense than water (1.00 g cm<sup>–³</sup>), so it forms the **upper** layer. Halogens are non-polar and far more soluble in cyclohexane than in water, so they concentrate in the upper layer
- Key cyclohexane-layer colours: Br<sub>2</sub> = orange; I<sub>2</sub> = purple/violet
- Upper layer purple/violet → I<sub>2</sub> → the original halide must have been KI:

Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KI → 2KCl + I<sub>2</sub>

**A** is incorrect as Cl<sub>2</sub> **does** oxidise Br<sup>–</sup> to Br<sub>2</sub>, but Br<sub>2</sub> in cyclohexane is **orange** (not purple); this distractor catches students who stop at "displacement occurred" without checking the colour

**B** is incorrect as Cl<sub>2</sub> and Cl<sup>–</sup> are the same element, no redox is possible; the cyclohexane layer would stay colourless

**C** is incorrect as F<sup>–</sup> cannot be oxidised by Cl<sub>2</sub> (fluorine is above chlorine in Group 7); no reaction occurs and the cyclohexane layer would stay colourless

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question combines three pieces of Group 7 knowledge, all three must be correct to land the answer:
> 
> - which halogen can oxidise which halide
> - the colour of each halogen in a non-polar solvent
> - which layer cyclohexane forms when added to water
> 
> Colours to memorise exactly, the January 2022 examiner report specifically flagged candidates writing "iodine is brown in cyclohexane" as a recurring error:
> 
> - **I**<sub>2</sub>** in cyclohexane** → purple / violet (pink also accepted)
> - **I**<sub>2</sub>** in water** → brown / yellow / pale orange
> - **Br**<sub>2</sub>** in cyclohexane** → orange (yellow, brown or red-brown also accepted)
> - **Br**<sub>2</sub>** in water** → orange / yellow / brown
> - **Cl**<sub>2</sub>** in cyclohexane** → pale green / near-colourless
> 
> Cyclohexane (density ≈ 0.78–0.79 g cm<sup>–³</sup>) is less dense than water (1.00 g cm<sup>–³</sup>), so it floats on top as the **upper** layer, where the halogen concentrates and gives the cleaner, more distinctive colour.
> 
> In structured (Section B) questions asking you to describe what you'd see, mark schemes require a **two-part** answer: **layer + colour** (e.g. "the upper / cyclohexane layer turns purple"). Giving the colour alone loses the layer mark, and vice versa.
